questions.q: What did Salesforce's own performance testing find about rendering large lists in LWC?
options: List size has no measurable effect on rendering performance
Rendering large record counts (in the thousands) directly into the DOM measurably slows the page down, while lists of roughly 50 rows or fewer render quickly
Only lists with fewer than 5 rows render correctly at all
Large lists only cause problems when combined with @wire
questions.explain: Salesforce's own testing found list size matters a great deal -- large lists (in the thousands of rows) rendered at once measurably slow the page, while lists around 50 rows or fewer render quickly.

questions.q: Why is `lwc:if={showAdvancedFilters}` described as a legitimate performance tool, not just a UI pattern?
options: Because content inside a false conditional block isn't instantiated into the DOM at all, so a child component inside it doesn't run its lifecycle hooks or fetch data until the condition becomes true
Because lwc:if automatically compresses the component's JavaScript bundle
Because lwc:if prevents the component from ever being included in the deployed package
Because lwc:if disables CSS rendering for hidden content
questions.explain: A conditional block that's currently false doesn't exist in the DOM, meaning any child component inside it doesn't instantiate, doesn't run connectedCallback(), and doesn't trigger any data fetching -- deferring real work, not just hiding it visually.

questions.q: Why is unconditional, expensive work inside `renderedCallback()` a performance risk, separate from the infinite-loop risk covered in Lesson 14?
options: renderedCallback() only runs once per component, so this isn't actually a risk
renderedCallback() runs after every render, not just the first one, so unconditional expensive work there repeats on every single re-render
renderedCallback() runs on a server, making any client-side cost irrelevant
Expensive work is never allowed inside any lifecycle hook
questions.explain: Because renderedCallback() fires after every render (not just the first), doing expensive work there unconditionally means that cost repeats every time the component re-renders -- the same guard pattern used for correctness also protects performance.

questions.q: What is the LWC equivalent of Apex's 'no SOQL or DML inside a loop' discipline, as described in this lesson?
options: Each child component in a rendered list should independently fetch its own data via its own Apex call
Fetch everything a list needs in one batched call before rendering, and pass the already-fetched data down into child components rather than letting each child fetch its own slice
Avoid using for:each entirely for any list longer than 10 items
Only use @wire, never imperative calls, to avoid any performance risk
questions.explain: Fetching data once per row (one Apex call per list item) multiplies a single reasonable request into many individual round trips -- the fix mirrors Apex bulkification: fetch once, in bulk, and distribute the data down to children.

questions.q: When does caching a getter's result in a plain field, rather than leaving the computation inside the getter, become the right fix?
options: Always -- getters should never be used for any computation
When the getter does meaningful work (like sorting or filtering a sizeable array) and is referenced from a template that re-renders frequently, making the repeated computation measurably expensive
Only when the getter is marked @api
Only when the getter returns a boolean value
questions.explain: Since a getter recomputes every time it's read, a computationally expensive getter referenced from a frequently re-rendering template can add measurable cost -- at that point, caching the derived result in a plain field (recomputed only when its real inputs change) is the appropriate fix.
